```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

# Load data
findex <- read_csv("data/GlobalFindexDatabase2025.csv")

# Filter to 2024 country-level aggregates for adults only.
# Exclude regional and income-group aggregates by dropping
# known aggregate codes from codewb.
findex_2024 <- findex %>%
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    group == "all"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !codewb %in% c("WLD", "LMY", "EAP", "ECA", "MNA", "SSA",
                   "LAC", "SAS", "HIC", "LIC", "LMC", "UMC")
  )

# Remove rows with missing key variables
analysis_data <- findex_2024 %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(account_t_d),
    !is.na(mobileaccount_t_d)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Clean region labels
    region_clean = case_when(
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "Sub-Saharan Africa")      ~ "Sub-Saharan Africa",
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "Europe & Central Asia")   ~ "Europe & Central Asia",
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "East Asia & Pacific")     ~ "East Asia & Pacific",
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "Latin America")           ~ "Latin America & Caribbean",
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "Middle East & North Africa") ~ "MENA",
      str_detect(regionwb24_hi, "South Asia")              ~ "South Asia",
      regionwb24_hi == "High income"                       ~ "High Income",
      TRUE                                                  ~ "Other"
    ),
    # Compute z-scores to identify statistical outliers
    mobile_zscore  = (mobileaccount_t_d - mean(mobileaccount_t_d)) /
                      sd(mobileaccount_t_d),
    account_zscore = (account_t_d - mean(account_t_d)) /
                      sd(account_t_d),
    # Convert to percentages for plotting
    account_pct = account_t_d * 100,
    mobile_pct  = mobileaccount_t_d * 100
  )

# Store global averages for reference lines
global_avg_account <- mean(analysis_data$account_t_d)
global_avg_mobile  <- mean(analysis_data$mobileaccount_t_d)

# Identify extreme outliers: |z-score| > 2 in either variable.
# These are the 8 countries labeled in the original PS2 figure.
outliers_to_label <- c(
  "Kenya", "Ghana", "Niger", "Chad",
  "Lebanon", "Mongolia", "Zambia", "Uganda"
)

labeled_countries <- analysis_data %>%
  filter(countrynewwb %in% outliers_to_label)

# Define consistent region colors matching original PS2
region_colors <- c(
  "Sub-Saharan Africa"     = "#E06C1F",
  "High Income"            = "#2A7F7F",
  "East Asia & Pacific"    = "#8B4789",
  "Latin America & Caribbean" = "#C8A400",
  "Europe & Central Asia"  = "#4A90A4",
  "MENA"                   = "#D45E5E",
  "South Asia"             = "#6BA368",
  "Other"                  = "#999999"
)
```

# Mobile Money Outliers in Global Financial Inclusion (2024)

Mobile money — financial services accessed via mobile phone rather
than a traditional bank — has expanded rapidly in the developing
world, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Yet adoption remains
highly uneven across countries, with some nations leading the world
while others in the same region remain severely excluded. This report
uses the World Bank Global Findex 2025 to identify countries that
are statistical outliers in mobile money adoption and overall
financial inclusion, and examines what patterns emerge.

# Data

The data come from the World Bank Global Findex 2025
(https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/globalfindex/download-data),
a nationally representative survey covering financial inclusion
indicators across over 140 economies in 2024. The unit of analysis
is the country. The two key variables are `account_t_d` (total
account ownership, share of adults) and `mobileaccount_t_d` (mobile
money account ownership, share of adults). Countries missing mobile
money data are excluded, leaving 80 countries with complete data.
Mobile money data is missing for most high-income countries, where
mobile money is negligible and the World Bank does not systematically
track it.

Outliers are identified using z-scores: a country is considered an
extreme outlier if its z-score exceeds $\pm 2$ on either variable,
placing it in approximately the top or bottom 2.5% of the
distribution.

# Results

```{r scatter-base}
# Base scatter plot: total account ownership (x) vs mobile money (y)
scatter_plot <- ggplot(
  analysis_data,
  aes(
    x     = account_pct,
    y     = mobile_pct,
    color = region_clean
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors) +
  # Reference lines at global averages
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = global_avg_mobile * 100,
    linetype   = "dashed",
    color      = "gray50",
    alpha      = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = global_avg_account * 100,
    linetype   = "dashed",
    color      = "gray50",
    alpha      = 0.5
  ) +
  # Quadrant annotations
  annotate(
    "text", x = 10, y = 78,
    label    = "Mobile-first\ninclusion",
    size     = 3,
    color    = "gray40",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 90, y = 78,
    label    = "Broad inclusion\n(mobile & bank)",
    size     = 3,
    color    = "gray40",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 10, y = 2,
    label    = "Low inclusion\noverall",
    size     = 3,
    color    = "gray40",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 90, y = 2,
    label    = "Traditional\nbanking dominates",
    size     = 3,
    color    = "gray40",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mobile Money Revolution: Extreme Outliers in Financial Inclusion (2024)",
    subtitle = "Africa Leads in Mobile Money While Traditional Banking Dominates Elsewhere",
    x        = "Total Account Ownership (%)",
    y        = "Mobile Money Account Ownership (%)",
    color    = "Region",
    caption  = "Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position  = "right",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r fig-scatter, fig.width=10, fig.height=6.5}
#| fig-cap: "Total account ownership vs. mobile money account ownership
#|   by country, 2024. Dashed lines mark global averages (61% total,
#|   31% mobile). Labeled countries are statistical outliers with
#|   z-scores exceeding ±2 on at least one variable. Sub-Saharan African
#|   countries (orange) dominate the mobile-first quadrant, while
#|   high-income countries (teal) cluster in the traditional banking
#|   quadrant."

# Add country labels for extreme outliers only
scatter_plot +
  geom_text_repel(
    data         = labeled_countries,
    aes(label    = countrynewwb),
    size         = 3.5,
    fontface     = "bold",
    box.padding  = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    segment.color = "gray50",
    max.overlaps  = 20,
    min.segment.length = 0
  )
```

The scatter plot reveals a striking geographic divide. Sub-Saharan
African countries dominate the upper-left quadrant — mobile-first
inclusion — with Kenya (90% total, 88% mobile) and Ghana as extreme
positive outliers in mobile money, achieving inclusion primarily
through non-bank channels. By contrast, Niger (15% total) and Chad
(21% total) sit in the lower-left as extreme negative outliers,
severely financially excluded despite being in the same macro-region
as the mobile money leaders.

Mongolia emerges as an outlier from a different direction: near-
universal account ownership (98%) achieved substantially through
mobile money (64%), showing that middle-income countries can
leapfrog traditional banking infrastructure. Lebanon stands out as
a middle-income MENA country with exceptionally low financial
inclusion (23% total, 3% mobile), reflecting its ongoing economic
collapse.

High-income countries (teal) cluster tightly in the lower-right —
traditional banking dominant, mobile money near zero — consistent
with the fact that the World Bank only collects mobile money data
where it is relevant.

# Conclusion

Mobile money has created a new pathway to financial inclusion, but
adoption remains highly uneven. The countries leading the mobile
money revolution and those most severely excluded often share the
same region — Sub-Saharan Africa — revealing that geography alone
cannot explain financial exclusion. Structural factors including
regulatory environments, infrastructure, and conflict appear to
drive the divergence. Understanding these outliers is increasingly
relevant as the World Bank and United Nations target universal
financial inclusion by 2030.
